> As engagement bait, as editorial aikido, I just marvel. There’s nothing more to say about it. Its existence is the comment.

Actually I don’t think [the NYT piece](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/opinion/writing-thinking-college-ai.html) is bait or troll, it is in fact the correct view of writing. It is not, and has never been, the only mode of critical thought, let alone the best one. It’s one of many modes that is effective in some circumstances. The article, ironically, reads like it was written by someone waking up from a  coma of uncritical writing fetishism:

> But what if we are mistaken in treating writing as the highest cultivation of thought? The evidence that supports this belief is thin at best. Writing can be useful cognitive scaffolding for memory and self-regulated learning, but the notion that it is the best process for developing thinking skills is a fairly recent idea, traceable to the 1970s writing-across-the-curriculum movement.

But then he slips right back into it, by retreating to orality and spoken disputation as the new gold standard, based on the thin evidence of an oral examination experiment in his classroom.

> In Plato’s “Phaedrus,” Socrates offers a startling criticism of writing. Written words, he claims, are not the true children of knowledge, because writing cannot speak, answer questions or come to its own defense. Only through conversation among minds, he suggests, does reason yield real insight. For the past two millenniums, this appraisal has seemed like a failure to appreciate the power of writing. But perhaps Socrates was right, and we think best by speaking, answering and defending our ideas

It’s still _linguistic_ supremacism if not _writing_ supremacism. Deeply blind to non-verbal intelligences.

Critical thinking is multimodal. Visual, mathematical, mechanical, even musical… there are many. Howard Gardner had a theory of multiple intelligences. And though the case for Goleman’s “emotional intelligence” is much weaker, there is something there too. None dominant generally in all situations. This is why the shape rotators vs. wordcel meme took off. I don’t like STEM-supremacism either, but it was much-needed pushback on the bs theory that critical thinking = writing.

I myself am a case in point. I’ve said I write to think, which is easily misunderstood. It’s just one of the ways I think, a late stage way in the development of an idea. Much of my upstream thinking is visual/diagrammatic or even straight-up mechanical, as in mechanical engineering intuitions developed through literal shape rotation. For example, the organizational analysis I’m best known for (Gervais Principle) probably reads like textual critical analysis of _The Office_ to verbal thinkers/linguistic supremacists, but it wasn’t. I _finished_ the thinking by writing, but I started it in shape-rotator land. It felt like opening the hood to examine the organizational engine. The evidence is all over. The key elements are a hierarchy and lifecycle diagram. The second part rests on a graph, and explicitly appeals to a Newtonian mechanics metaphor.

To the extent I do critical thinking, it’s mostly non-verbal. Words are just the UI. The verbal part of the thinking is crafting a story and conveying emotions with good rhetoric. It’s not where the ideas themselves took shape.

In fact purely textual critical thinking usually strikes me as incredibly shallow and hopelessly lost within whatever tradition it situates itself in.
